questions.q: Why does back-of-the-envelope estimation matter especially for this platform?
options: This platform has the lowest data volume of any case study in this chapter
The defining challenge is raw volume — billions of engagement events a day, with viral moments spiking that unevenly on specific posts
Estimation only matters for batch systems, never streaming ones
Estimation is irrelevant since social media platforms have no real scale concerns
questions.explain: The scale itself, and the unevenness of a viral spike, is the core design problem here.

questions.q: Why does sharding by content_id, rather than by time bucket, matter for a viral post?
options: Sharding strategy has no effect on how viral posts are handled
Sharding by hashed content_id spreads even a viral post's writes across many shards, instead of piling them onto one time-bucket shard
content_id sharding is only relevant for nightly batch jobs
Time-bucket sharding always performs better than content_id sharding
questions.explain: A time-bucket-only shard would concentrate an entire viral post's write volume onto a single shard.

questions.q: Why is the trending-content leaderboard described as a textbook caching use case?
options: Caching a leaderboard has no performance benefit over recomputing it per request
Leaderboards should never be cached because they change too frequently
The leaderboard is written far more often than it's read
It's read enormously more often than it's written, and the underlying counts change comparatively slowly
questions.explain: Refreshing the cache every 10-15 seconds and serving reads from it avoids recomputing the same aggregate on every request.

questions.q: Why does this platform lean AP, consistent with Lesson 19's CAP analysis?
options: This platform requires perfectly consistent counts at all times
CAP theorem does not apply to social media systems
A like count that's a few seconds stale is invisible to users, while a pipeline going down during a spike is very visible — so availability wins
AP systems always have zero staleness by definition
questions.explain: The consumer tolerates staleness completely, so there's no reason to sacrifice availability chasing precision nobody needs.

questions.q: What is the actual defining challenge that distinguishes this case study from the others in the chapter?
options: The need for perfectly consistent, never-stale data at all times
A requirement for siloed, per-tenant infrastructure
The complete absence of any streaming components
Raw ingestion volume and handling an uneven, spike-prone write pattern concentrated on individual pieces of content
questions.explain: Unlike the other case studies, the core problem here is volume and hot-key write concentration, not logical or consistency complexity.
